review: When I first purchased this game my friend told me that he didn't think that I could fully experience it to it's potential because I am in a wheelchair. He was wrong. I beat the story mode and enjoyed it thoroughly. The combat was one of my favorite things. Even with access to guns, melee was totally viable unlike in other games I have played. The physics were also outstanding. It was so satisfying to be able to touch and move almost anything you wanted to. At times it was a little irritating with your arms or guns getting stuck on things like corners or bars but that is the only complaint I have. This game is amazing and I would recommend it to anyone who has VR.

Wow... It actually lived up to the hype. Amazing physics.

I didn't like Boneworks at first. It's not exactly like the other VR games I've played. In fact it was only after 6 hours of play time that I finally decided to check what other people were saying about it. [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7irWC2uXuSY]And this was the video that I watched.[/url]

That's when something finally clicked in my head and I realized what Boneworks is all about. It's not about the protagonist, but you, the player! Boneworks is designed for you to be able to express yourself and do the most wicked stuff in it. Everything from parkouring your way around the level, to taking down multiple enemies at the same time in slow motion, to shooting yourself in the foot and dying. I did all of those things, and a lot more.

Boneworks isn't the type of game you take seriously or try to "play it by the rules". This is a simulation, and you are Neo, there are no rules. In fact even the tutorial part of the game mentions that you can complete a level any way you want, even by cheating your way to the end.

The story and characters don't matter here, it's not that kind of game. Instead Boneworks offers [b]the best[/b] interactive sandbox VR experience. Not all the levels are equally fun to play, but they're all unique. And they serve to introduce the player to new gameplay mechanics, and challenge their creativity. 

As mentioned before, there are no rules in Boneworks. Any object can be used as a weapon or a shield. Even your dead enemies' lifeless corpses can be picked up and swung or thrown or used as barriers against incoming bullets. You can scale practically any building, and later on you'll be able to stick to walls and even fly. There's tons of secrets and loot everywhere, so exploration is highly recommended and rewarding.

Gunplay, and especially the slow-motion shootouts are immensely satisfying. [url=https://imgur.com/y96RZxt]Here's me Max Payne-ing some poor bastard.[/url] Tons of guns, attachments and weapon combinations. You can dual wield, you can grab enemies and throw them around, you can barricade doors or crack their skulls with a watermelon. 

The game itself isn't very hard, so you're never in any real danger. Which in turn allows you to be as creative and as entertaining as you want to be. But that's not to say that it's a game that I would recommend to VR newbies. If you just got a VR headset and you're considering buying Boneworks because it's on sale - buy it. But play something else first, like Beat Saber or Until You Fall or Super Hot. And then come back to this when you're ready. Because Boneworks can be a little bit overwhelming to a new player. It's not a 'party game' that you let your friends take turns playing. It takes some getting used to, and some elements like navigation and parkour will take a longer time to master, at least in my experience.

Visually, Boneworks looks good! It's a game that chose clarity over fluff, and it's still a very pleasant experience. In no small part thanks to it's amazing physics simulation and sound design. And did I mention that Boneworks has a killer soundtrack? I did not expect that at all, especially from a first person VR shooter game. Sometimes I would dread the thought of leaving a level because the music was so good.

[url=https://imgur.com/sMxLn5f][here's another short clip of me messing around][/url]

Things that I didn't really like? I guess I wish the save system worked differently. I was hoping that once I finished the game, I would be able to go back to any level with all my resources and gear unlocked. Because I worked really hard to collect everything and get all the guns. But instead, if you load an earlier level, you don't 'travel' there, you just load a save game from 20 hours ago. Where you don't have anything again. It was just a bit disappointing, it's no big deal. And maybe most players actually like this idea.

In conclusion, I think that Boneworks is a must-have title for any VR enthusiast. It's got advanced VR mechanics, satisfying gameplay, great soundtrack and universal physical interactivity, as well as a bunch of additional free content. The only thing that would make this game better would be some kind of coop or multiplayer mode. [i](This can actually be achieved with mods now!)[/i]

Stress Level Zero did a phenomenal job creating one of my favorite VR games, and I can't wait to see what they come up with next!

This is not just any other VR game, this is revolutionary, a pioneer in free locomotion VR games. You push on the wall and you don't just go through like in other games, instead you push yourself away. You are an object, the same as everything else. You are affected by physics. You aren't just a floating head with hands, you have a body, and you can move and climb and jump on things. The other thing about this game that a lot of people discredit is the story. They say this game barely has a plot, but there is a plot, its there, you just have to look for it, read the writing on the walls, piece together what you know and what you see to get the full picture.
That being said, do not get this game if you find yourself getting sick in VR. Play other games until you get over that hump of motion sickness. Once you do adapt, get this game immediately. You wont regret it.

Beat the game on launch day. This game is the best VR game I own hands down. I would say more but it is 2 am and I need sleep.

Get this game.

You'll see a lot of reviews saying this is the best VR game ever, which can brush over your head.

But let me tell you why, in my opinion this is currently one of the most revolutionary VR experiences you can get your hands on.

<<<The Good>>>
Boneworks has one of the most passionate, talented, and skilled VR indie devs behind it. Stress Level Zero have aimed to innovate and make VR better, rather than sticking to what is safe and known already. This game is a result of that ambition, and it really shows in the quality of the entire experience.

The physics in this game feel spectacular, even if you don't have any actual haptic feedback, you still "feel" the weight of objects. They've had a good balance of where you hands ARE and where your hands WOULD be if you actually felt the weight, and it tricks your brain in all the best ways. They've taken the time to fine-tune the strength of your character, the strength of materials and objects, and the strength of enemies into account, and it all feels real. I think the best example of this is I didn't even notice how good they were, because it all felt so intuitive initially. 

The level designs are intricately detailed, full of secrets, and well paced. Each level is unique and interesting to go through, and the amount of replayability is really nice (especially in later Story levels, as there are several corridors to potentially explore). I never got bored on my first run through, and still don't as I look for all the secrets I can (and some are really well hidden!) and I'm always discovering new little things about the game and the levels I go through. 
To add on this, the Story of this game is told through the levels, things written on the walls, and the way things function. There are displays, things written by things before you, and just a few other things that keep the mystery of the world going, and it creates an answer in everyone's head differently, without the game necessarily telling you what's happening 100%. It's nice, and it's good to have levels that aren't there for flavor text. The journey you go on has a reason and everything that exists within MythOS assembles itself in a story that starts making sense when you take the time to thoroughly look through the levels.

As previously mentioned, what encourages you to find secrets is the fun to be had in the Sandbox mode, which you can unlock different NPCs and objects by finding them in secret boxes hidden around levels, and thrown into reclamation bins. It's fun trying to figure out things, especially since there are very few guides or videos on it, so finding something feels like a "first-time" experience because you haven't heard about it from anywhere else.
 
The Arena mode is a great touch to really go against the AI in a focused setting and the challenges are different enough and make sense given the game's use of physics. It feels satisfying to complete your first Hard difficulty challenge, and even if the spawns are the same, each fight feels unique and engaging.

When you hit something, it HITS and it feels satisfying every time you nail something in the head. The shooting as well feels satisfying and doesn't feel too punishing with recoil at all. Both of these are enhanced by the Slow Motion button you have on your left controller, which tapped (once - x2 slowed, twice x4 slowed, thrice x8 slowed) feels absolutely amazing and makes you feel like an action hero at times. This can also aid in tight situations in arena or the Story, as it can give you a second to think about what to do without necessarily having to pause (which you can't anyway) but it's a satisfying and welcome feature that I miss in other games of a similar scope and style. 

The Sound Design and Soundtrack are masterful. There's not much else to say other than it fully immerses you and grounds you in the world. The ambiance can make an area feel comfortable or intimidating and the soundtrack really helps the mood of it. This is with any soundtrack though, so gushing about how amazing it is, is sorta pointless :)

<<<The 'Bad'>>>
As with any video game real time physics, you WILL have some inconsistencies. Things get stuck in awkward ways, your arms go through objects more than you may like, and stuff can get caught on your character, leading to some awkward moments. This isn't a dealbreaker, but it's noticeable enough to mention. But to me, that adds to the charm and fun of the game. If EVERYTHING did how I wanted, it wouldnt be Boneworks, because I'm using logic from other games that let you flail everything like a paperweight and pass through walls and objects, and your person with ease. It MAKES you think about how you're handling something, just like you would IRL. 

That's it really, no other complaints with this game.

<<<Conclusion>>>
"But Ki" I hear you say. "This sounds like any standard game with physics, what's so special about Boneworks?"
VR my friend, VR is what makes a physics game fully click and immersive. This is one of the first times I genuinely got fully immersed given all the reasons previously stated. It's as unforgettable as Half Life, and if you were awed by the first time you took the tram through the facility, this game will give you that same feeling ten-fold.

Few bugs, great physics, soundtrack, gameplay, pacing, AI, etc.
All make for a game I simply have to keep playing, and I'm excited to see where SL0 takes this game further.

9.5/10

I'm a Dad to twins with a really busy life and I rarely get to REALLY get into a game, I've found myself setting an alarm to get half an hour in with Boneworks before the kids wake up, which to anyone else in the same position is review enough in itself!

For everyone else, this is an absolutely brilliant game, one of the few on VR that I have been excited to get back into every day and the first time I've been genuinely wowed by physics puzzles since firing up HL2. In short, in Boneworks' world, if you think it could be possible, it usually is. 

The obvious comparison product is Half Life Alyx, which is a smooth, polished VR experience BUT, despite its brilliance, Alyx still feels like it's on rails and designed to move you from moment to moment as a tech demo with the illusion of freedom. Boneworks has more of the old school Half Life ethos where you see a distant door and how you get there is up to you and breaking the rules and taking a different path to the obvious is part of the experience (and often rewarded too). Beyond the 15 hour or so story line, there are sandboxes, arenas, challenges and much more to check out that make this exceptional value for money. 

There are places where Boneworks falls down, the first is the use of both hands at once; climbing and manipulating larger objects (like crates and barrels), both feel like you're fighting the engine, rather than working with it, though this is likely down to the limitations of the controller tracking through the Oculus Quest I used to play. 

The second is the inventory system, which relies on placing items into predefined holsters about your body by letting go of them in the right location. Great idea, but again, poor tracking occasionally leads to a prized weapon being dropped during a fight, or worse, falling into one of the games many abysses, never to be seen again. One especially frustrating moment involved dropping a flashlight during a dark tunnel sequence and having to load an earlier save. 

These minor gripes aside, Boneworks is really worth a play and represents one of the few complete VR single player experiences, and one with good replay value, on several occasions having completed a tricky puzzle, I realised that the devs had hidden a short cut in plain view (like a climbable pipe or hidden walkway) and I'm already curious as to where they all lead!

The continued addition of extra content is appreciated too and I look forward to checking out the Zombie Arena that dropped this week. 

An absolute gem, at a reasonable price and well worth a look.

I've owned VR for around two years now and this is the best game I've played by a long shot. One of the biggest things in this game is the amazing reverse kinematics (The body simulated in game). It's really good at fooling your brain into thinking that you are actually a part of the game. There's also plenty of attention to detail when it comes to the aspects that matter. The gun reloads aren't finicky and don't result in your controllers slamming together, inside out tracking (I use the HP WMR headset) still handles reloads behind the back *really* well (Which was one of my primary concerns), and the puzzle construction brings me back to the moments of playing portal. Personally I got around 17 hours of game play out of the campaign and I enjoyed every minute. Even after the campaign I still go back to it for the experience and the area modes. Amazing work from the developers here at Stress Level Zero. This is the kickoff of VR experiences that I would call serious out-of-life experiences.

Every good game has it's downsides, and here it's the lack of mid-level saves, which I have no doubt they'll fix in upcoming updates. They do leave a disclaimer stating that this game is for experienced VR users and I do have to say this is true to some extent. The biggest downside I experienced personally was the motion sickness, but it only lasted the first two days or so of playing the game. (It only happened for me after a few hours of game play) Being one in the crowd of those who experienced the support issues with the WMR headsets on launch day I can definitely vouch for their attention to fixing issues quickly and effectively while keeping those who are affected extremely well updated.
Taking a break from video games after I've played this one, so terrifyingly realistic... Just thinking about how I incapacitated that zombie by shoving a crowbar up it's ass gives me chills...

I’m glad I procrastinated until the release of Half-Life: Alyx (HL:A) to finally review Boneworks.  As much as I love HL:A (IMO it is easily the best game in VR, and I’ve played nearly everything out there), it has still made me even more impressed by what the small team of 10 developers at Stress Level Zero were able to accomplish here.  That is: A truly full-featured system of physics-based VR game mechanics that give you nearly complete freedom, ability, and control over your character and environment.  And, in addition to sandbox and arena modes, they crafted a pretty damn nifty little single-player game as well.  To me, they have achieved the closest thing yet to how I always imagined VR to be: The feeling of being transported inside another world, truly embodying a virtual character in an artificial space.
You may have heard a lot of griping about what Boneworks lacks in terms of a polished, story-driven, single-player action game.  You know what?  It’s all true.  Level design is inconsistent, varying from excellent/inspired to bland or just sorely lacking.  Enemies are visually boring and have simplistic AI, making combat encounters rarely interesting or challenging (the exception is the robotic “crablet” which is pretty damn cool).  Graphically it is on a solid foundation (weapons are fantastic) and occasionally looks great but it lacks any real sense of art direction and has iffy performance in certain areas.  The story, sadly, is simply incomprehensible and poorly told.  It feels like there might have been some pretty interesting ideas in there, but they simply never figured out how to express them properly.
However, at the end of the day, I just really don’t give a ****.  I love this game and consider it one of the most innovative and entertaining experiences I’ve ever had in gaming.  The fun of Boneworks is that it is so completely and consistently physical and interactive.  Most VR titles deal heavily in abstraction and only let you interact with a few predetermined items.  Boneworks achieves consistency: Everything can be grabbed, pushed, climbed, thrown etc.  Its fully realized physics system makes you feel like you are inside an alternate reality.   You can walk, sprint, jump, crouch, and clamber up almost anything.  Every object can be picked up, stored/holstered, thrown, swung, dropped, etc.  NPC’s can be interacted with physically DURING combat, not just as lifeless ragdolls as in HL:A.  Like, you can grab an enemy’s arm as it’s slapping at you and pull it to the ground.  Or grab a leg and flip it over, watching as they flail around to get back up.  It’s amazing!  Your character also has weight and momentum.  You can sprint to an enemy and hockey-check into them with appropriate force.  Guns are not fused to your arm but simply exist as physical objects in the world.  You can throw them, holster them, toss them to the other hand, or use them as melee weapons.  Almost all of this is totally intuitive.  Once you figure out the basic controls, you feel empowered to simply use your hands and arms as you would in the real world, and rarely will Boneworks disappoint you by making you realize, “nah, can’t do this, it’s just a videogame.”   
So, in VR, what does all of this achieve?  Immersion.   HL:A shows how immersive AAA graphics, sound, and highly refined hand interactions can make VR.  Unfortunately, some of the limited mechanics in HL:A detract from immersion.  For example, you feel like you should be able to grab onto a top shelf and pull yourself up to see what’s on top…but you can’t.  You can’t climb anything, only ladders.  You feel like you should be able to pick up a pipe and hit a zombie with it.  You can’t.  In Boneworks it’s the opposite.  The sometimes janky interactions, weak sound design, and less impressive visuals detract.  But the mechanics absolutely enhance immersion because it has such a consistent, high level of interaction with every aspect of the environment that with time the act of playing becomes second-nature.  You simply imagine what you want to do and you just act it out.  Want to throw your empty gun at the NPC? Want to just throw a punch?  Go ahead, it all works.  Want to jump over that ledge and grab that rope hanging in the air.  Just do it.  Amazing.
What is so special about this design is that it unlocks your creativity as a player.  There was one area where a ledge was just out of reach above me so I couldn’t cling onto it and pull myself up.  I could have pushed over a box to use to give me a step up.  But, I happened to have a long-handled axe.  So, I reached up with the axe held at the very bottom of the handle and hooked the axe-head over the lip of the ledge.  Then, I pulled myself up the axe handle (you have superhuman grip and strength, thankfully), allowing me to reach the edge and pull myself up.  Wow.  Go try to do that in other VR games and see how far you get.  Your weapon will just clip through everything and you’ll need to go find a special “interactable” ladder to climb.  Not in Boneworks.  Anything can be a ladder, anything can be climbed, anything can be a weapon.  Sure, sometimes it can be a tad janky or glitchy, but no two people will ever play through a Boneworks level in exactly the same way, and that is a truly special achievement by the developers, and so rare in gaming today.
I am so excited by what is to come from SLZ in the future.  They have put in so much hard work to lay an incredible foundation for future VR games.  Now, they just need to build on this and they will have something truly special.  I salivate at the thought of these game mechanics merging with better game-design, more challenging combat, and better art/graphics.  Again, none of these aspects here are terrible (this is a solid, fun game), they just have a ton of room for improvement.  For the time being, I will continue to have a blast experimenting with Boneworks while patiently awaiting what SLZ comes up with next.

I got Boneworks when I first got my Oculus Quest 2. This game is probably one of my favorite VR games that I own. Whenever you want to have fun either in sandbox mode or story mode, it doesn't matter both of them will be fun to play no matter what you do.

Boneworks is an amazing game, probably one of my current favorite vr games alongside blade and sorcery. The story, although kind of vague, is pretty cool and the missions are pretty fun to play through.

While playing Boneworks, most puzzles and combat scenarios can be played however you want. If you're fighting an enemy you can use guns, melee weapons, grabbable objects, or even just slam your foes into the wall and beat them to a pulp and in puzzle scenarios there are typically multiple ways to solve or sometimes even skip puzzles (with a few exceptions) and portions of levels if you utilize objects in your surroundings and/or find things to climb over, but in early playthroughs those can have consequences as you can skip over collectable items too such as weapons or sandbox items/npcs to reclaim for the sandbox mode. It really pays off to explore and experiment in every inch of the game.

Aside from the main story missions, there are also modes like sandbox and arena. Arena is pretty self explanatory, gather weapons and ammo in a starting room and select some sort of mode or custom waves to fight against. You can choose preset modes or choose what enemies you want to fight and how many of them there are. Zombies is another arena mode too where you fight against waves of zombies in a warehouse and find weapons and board up windows. There's also Sandbox which is where the game really shines after you've done pretty much everything else. You can test out different weapons you've reclaimed, fight enemies you've gotten, and just do all sorts of wacky stuff and experimenting with what you can and can't do with most objects. Eventually you might get tired of having the same things over and over from the base game though, and that can be fixed with modding. Boneworks has probably hundreds of mods already available with a bunch of different custom player models, gadgets, weapons, vehicles, NPCs, maps, etc. and with everything unlocked it's pretty much like Gmod VR. On top of that there is also a multiplayer mod, which last I checked was a bit janky but there's been a few updates since I last played so could be better now.

With the mods, sandbox, main story, arena modes, and custom maps boneworks is almost infinitely replayable and has so much to do that it's hard to get bored with it. There are still a good few things I haven't touched on or elaborated here that are better experienced in the game rather than told and it's 110% worth it to get boneworks.

Definitely one of the best VR games, and one of the best games in general I have ever played. Even after completing the story multiple times and sandboxing for hours, there is still so much to do. Where many VR games just give you a gun and make you shoot the enemies in a slow-paced manner, Boneworks gives you a large level filled to the brim with physics objects, firearms, melee weapons and puzzles, giving you all the freedom to get creative. Just shooting the enemy is boring? Well, drop a brick on them from a four-story building you just climbed onto. The possibilities are endless. Especially the physics aspects as well as the overall "atmosphere" of the game really gives it that Portal / Half-Life feel we all know and love. The levels are so detailed that even after playing them multiple times, I still keep finding new things, collectibles, hidden areas, new routes, etc. The arena modes are also endlessly entertaining. Combine some gunplay with the easy-to-use slow-mo button and you got yourself a true John Wick feeling. I could go on for hours naming everything thats great about this game, but all in all, it's a perfect game that I can definitely recommend, 10/10. This game is really fun. You can mess around in sandbox, do campaign, or become a gladiator in arena mode. The game can be really odd sometimes, but that's what makes it fun.

here are some fun things you can do if you get bored:

-Go back through the campaign and try to get all ammo possible (to unlock the Utility Gun and Nimbus Gun on the time tower)

-Get a power puncher and punch yourself

-Go back through the campaign and unlock the secret items littered across each level (including a katana)

-Go into sandbox and create custom missions / scenarios

-Download mods on the Bonetome (trust me its worth it)

One critique I have the fact that you have to use 3rd party software to add mods. They should really consider adding the steam workshop to this game.

[b]In short:[/b] Boneworks is one of my favourite games of all time and probably one of the best games for VR to date.

[b]In detail:[/b]
The game isn't perfect, far from it actually. Interactions are often janky, performance isn't too great and collecting some things can be really tiresome. None of those can actually taint the experience though. Physics are incredibly immersive (my friends spend at least an hour each in the Breakroom before the actual tutorial). Weapons are distinct and feel natural after a short while. The inventory system is easy to use and doesn't let you take out your items periodically. While the story isn't as well-written as HL:A, it's definitely intriguing and unexpected.

On the subject of the campaign: it's around 9 hours, which isn't too great for a single player flatscreen game, but compared to other FPSs it's not too bad. Additionally, this only accounts playing through it once. On top of that you unlock the Arena mode, which lets you battle infinite waves of enemies or predetermined challenges with unlocked weapons. When it comes to collectables, there are a lot of them. Every level of the story mode holds at least a few weapon unlocks and many Sandbox mode unlocks.

Sandbox is akin to Garry's Mod. You get a utility gun and can spawn anything you've unlocked in the campaign. Redacted chamber and Hover Junkers don't have it, but instead offer you a smaller, standalone experience and let you unlock additional items.

Lastly we have the Zombie Warehouse - COD Zombies in VR. It's well made, melee weapons are scattered across the map. Utilities, guns and map expansions cost you ammo which you gain from kills. The mode also features the Board Gun which allows you to make barricades and play more tactically.

In conclusion: the game is a lot more than just a great campaign. If you want to unlock everything or at least the most interesting items, like the noclip gun, or the Utility Gun for the campaign, you'll play through it at least twice. [h1][b] Why Boneworks made my first 10/10 [/b]
[/h1]

When I first played [i]Boneworks[/i] I took it for granted. Then again, I agree with almost everything that I said in my first review, although things like combat with blunt weapons and optimization have been greatly improved. Even then I still thought it was the best VR game at the time, but then I thought [i]Half Life: Alyx[/i] would make me ditch the game.

Then [i]Half Life: Alyx[/i] comes around. I played it. I enjoyed it. But there was always something missing when I was playing. The story was nice and the gunplay was fun, but the environments around me felt static. I could pick things up and play with them, like using a marker on a pane of glass, but I couldn't climb, run, shove enemies down, or even hit them with a crowbar. In [i]Boneworks[/i], you could do all those things as long as you were okay with the jank that came with it.

I still consider [i]Half Life: Alyx[/i] to be the best VR game out there for everyone, but it wasn't the best game for me. I wanted something more. I wanted to do more. [i]Boneworks[/i] was there to give me more. [i]Half Life: Alyx[/i] only contained a static landscape that was limited in exploration, while [i]Boneworks[/i] lets you break the game for fun if you tried hard enough. By sacrificing polish and comfort, [i]Boneworks[/i] gave you freedom. 

Its not perfect. I would say [i]Half Life: Alyx[/i] is closer to perfect. But the experience that [i]Boneworks[/i] provides you cannot find in any VR game out there.

Genuinely my favourite VR game, by a wide margin. Overtaking Alyx, Blade and Sorcery, Robo Recall, Beatsaber, Pavlov all the classics. I cannot overstate how much more right than all the others this game feels one it all comes together and how much attention to detail there is in it. It's the full package: 

Because of the momentum and the full body simulation, the immersion is fantastic, this where Boneworks exceeds all the other VR games by the greatest margins. No glitching through objects, no feet hanging in mid air like magic. No weird crab walks when you duck. Everything works as you feel like it should in reality. Before you jump your character ducks a little, and if you duck lower and throw your hands up in sync you'll jump higher. Try to put your hands through a wall and instead of just flopping against it you'll push your whole body back like you're doing a wall push-off. Try to run on a wheeled cart or imbalanced object and you'll roll it backwards underneath you as and split the difference in momentum. My only slight gripe is trying to walk on big piles of loose rubble (or bodies) can make you feel like a baby giraffe as your character slips and slides trying to find their footing.

The puzzles are fun (often multiple solutions, a big plus) the physics simulation is used to brilliant effect in lots of places. Some puzzles feel like Human Fall Flat, except you have full body control instead of some QWOP like handicap at moving things. There's little clues scattered around to both the puzzles and lots of little easter eggs and secrets. And a nice smattering of lore stashed on notepads and graffiti'd on the world if you like to look at the little details.

The platforming is also fantastic. Because of the aforementioned immersion and simulation, the way you never hover anywhere and you can use your arms to adjust momentum, they just feel so good. Balancing and shimmying along a narrow ledge will feel properly tense, making a running leap for that swinging rope will feel amazing when you grab it and your arms whip up and your body starts swinging, and leaping over boxes and tipping over stacks of shelves as you go to dodge the hoard of angry NPCs behind will feel very cinematic. If you had the sensors for full body tracking I bet it would be even more incredible.

The melee is good. In isolation it doesn't feel quite as fun as B&S, but it's pretty damn close, and that's probably just because Boneworks is less of an insane power trip where you're not strong enough to punch people into orbit with your bare hands. And I'm a huge fan of the full body collision Boneworks has, meaning the enemies can't just float through you if you collide like they always do in B&S and ruin the flow. Again the inertia simulation aspect adds a lot to the melee, as you grab enemies and throw them around you'll also end up shifting your own body around in relation to them, and if you charge into someone or do a running skewer or you'll actually lose full-body movement speed as you make contact. Even the grip friction is simulated and analogue, if you stab something hard enough with a long handled weapon, your grip will slide along the shaft as you try to push forward, and the harder you hold the grip function on your controllers the stronger your in-game grip is.

The shooting is very satisfying all on its own, easily as fun as Pavlov's or Alyx's, and the weight/momentum and collision simulation really adds another extra layer to small vs big weapon CQC techniques. The core gun variety isn't huge, obviously way better than Alyx's 3 but not a gun smorgasbord like Pavlov, and there's weapon variants with differing attachments/sights to keep things fresher. Again the attention to detail shines, there's one deliberately very dark level in the story mode, and you'll suddenly realise how big of a difference actual glow in the dark sights makes to gun utility, nevermind the flashlight mounted weapons. BUT, and this is the biggest, best but you'll ever see; the gunplay feels great, in a game that also has good melee combat! Pavlov and Alex don't hold a candle to Boneworks when it come's to John Wick'ing your way through a hoard of shmucks. Knocking people over and popping heads as you hold them in an arm lock, blocking a swing with your rifle slamming them with the buttstock and nailing them as they fall over, flipping helmets off with a pistol whip and doming them on the return stroke, they all feel so badass. And you even have slo-mo to really nail the execution.

My biggest criticism is the game's campaign gets off to a very slow start, and it gatelocks all the really fun sandbox content until you reach/find certain milestones in the campaign mode. And it's understandable because the game itself takes a good bit of time to understand and to learn to use the fully reactive simulation aspects, so the first few levels are more or less playgrounds to try out the physics and movement options. And that's enough fun on its own with lots of little secret detours that you could easily spend several hours messing around before you even get your first gun, and another couple of hours after that before you really get to see the game shine when it puts everything together in more complex levels with actually serious enemies.

Oh and if you get VR motion sickness, this is definitely a game you'll have to acclimatize to. Mine is only mild, but in my first few play sessions of Boneworks it was definitely noticeable. But on the plus side, once you get used to it in Boneworks, you'll be basically immune to the feeble motion sickness of lesser games.

[h1]🎮Half-Life + Portal + Garry’s Mod, in VR[/h1]
Minus the excellent storytelling, BONEWORKS could easily pass as a Valve-made game. It clearly has the fingerprints of both Half-Life, Portal, Garry’s Mod all over it. Half-Life and Portal for the atmosphere; trapped all alone in a bleak, mysterious world, progressing through the map little by little. A mix of all three for the gameplay: equipped with a realistic physics engine; and the manipulation of said engine for combat, solving physics puzzles, or simply just messing around in its sandbox world.

[h1]🏔️Setting and Style[/h1] 
BONEWORKS is set in itself, a fictional engine also called “Boneworks”, running an operating system called MythOS which is a virtual city. You travel through the different levels set in MythOS, solving different types of puzzles to progress.

The levels clearly have a “game under development” or “work-in-progress” aesthetic with its chaotic artstyle, generic gridlike floors, and wireframe / robotic models for NPCs. Because of this unique aesthetic and virtual reality setting, BONEWORKS clearly got away from the hassle of creating fully finished and lifelike set pieces, and also makes all the genuine in-game bugs and glitches quite bearable.

[h1]⚙️The realism and physics engine[/h1]
Despite the “work-in-progress” aesthetic of its virtual world, BONEWORKS is quite high on the realism scale of video games. Almost everything can be picked up, thrown, and manipulated. Objects like boxes, glasswares, and electronics are destructible. Various types of weapons to use: Sledgehammers, Crowbars, Baseball Bats, Knives, Swords, Automatic Guns, Pistols, and many more. Combat is just as realistic. Weapon handling and melee combat is on par or even better than other VR contemporaries. There is gun recoil, manual reloading (where I find quite inconsistent), and believable haptics. Melee combat requires actual swings and stabs to inflict damage.

All objects have different weights and are well simulated by the game for VR gameplay, both in its physical characteristics and in handling. It is as authentic as it can be, and pushes the VR platform to another level when it comes to interaction with the virtual world. This results in a fun, unscripted, and spontaneous sandbox gameplay experience. It’s not perfect though, as sometimes you will encounter physics bugs: body parts getting stuck to walls, objects clipping and getting tangled with each other, among other examples. 

Going for realism, they naturally decided to implement fully rendered arms, feet, and bodies, and they work fine to an extent. To provide that sense of realism that the developers wanted to convey. Visually it’s very realistic. In practice, it’s not the most immersive experience; your arms get clunky all the time as only the hands have actual tracking. 

Both your virtual arms and body constantly block your view and it messes with the immersion when you see them not in sync with your actual arms and body. This is also the case when using moving around and you notice your virtual feet walking / running while you’re actually just standing still or seating. I wish there was an option to hide them and render just the hands like in Half-Life: Alyx.

The inventory system is typical. Two slots for each shoulder, three slots around your body plus an ammo pouch. It’s not as accurate as I wanted it to be, sometimes I get the wrong things out of my body and I fail to pick up/slot objects on my shoulders, but it’s fine for the most part. You can also access an exploded view of the inventory by using the quick menu for a more convenient operation, a fine little neat feature that all VR games should game.

[h1]🧩Puzzle-Platformer[/h1]
The main gameplay element of BONEWORKS is its puzzle solving mechanics combined with platformer gameplay to progress through the levels. Most of the levels themselves are just one big physics playground that you need to solve through the use of mainly the physics engine: manipulation, pushing, pulling, throwing, running, and jumping around the world. 

The puzzles are clearly inspired by Half-Life and Portal. From stacking up boxes to reach the next area, or putting some heavy objects to human-sized floor buttons to keep doors open. Thanks to VR, you are really immersed in the scale of the levels. Falling from great heights seems more terrifying now, jumping through obstacles are more tense than ever.

[h1]😵Niche in a Niche - extreme comfort levels[/h1]
With VR gaming already as niche as it is right now, promoting it as a ”VR experts only” game makes it even more niche, and rightfully so. It certainly requires previous VR experience to quickly familiarize with the game mechanics and develop resistance to VR sickness. It is  definitely not for everyone. 

Combined with the aforementioned fully rendered arms, feet, and body, there is no teleportation movement, only full locomotion movement. Buyer beware for those who cannot handle full locomotion. There is a jump mechanic in the game and works just as any other game. You just press a button to jump, though there is a slight delay. All these along with the already platformer and “jumpy” nature of the game, adds up and results in a very uncomfortable experience for me. I had my own share of VR sickness while playing, as opposed to other games like Half-Life: Alyx, or The Walking Dead: Saints and Sinners, where I could play for hours at a time without discomfort.

[h1]📖Story and Characters[/h1]
The weakest part of BONEWORKS. It almost has no story in it and does little to entice players or give them reason to advance the game from a story standpoint. The plot itself is very vague and ambiguous, maybe to save the writers the trouble of having to write an actual plot. 

There’s hardly any characters in BONEWORKS, and they are all forgettable, unessential, and have zero personality. You probably won't even remember their names while playing throughout the game, including the main character. Enemies are also as generic as they can be. 

[h1]🖥️Technical Performance[/h1]
The game runs smoothly even with the resolution set to 120% on my rig: i7-8700k, 32GB RAM, and GTX 1080. No crashes, game-breaking bugs, or major glitches I've encountered. Using an Oculus Quest with ALVR, I was able to play wirelessly and use the movement scheme to its fullest, without analog turning. Graphics are beautiful for a VR game although the textures are noticeable a bit low quality resolution wise.

[h1]⚖️Conclusion[/h1]
BONEWORKS pushes the VR platform to another level when it comes to interaction with the virtual world. A fun and spontaneous sandbox VR platformer. I recommend this game, only if you can handle its extreme comfort levels and already have substantial experience with VR games.

I holstered my ax and turned around to find another one leaping toward me. I reached up quick enough to grab it with both hands while it was mid flight, and proceeded to bash it against a concrete wall until it was deactivated.

This has been a great glimpse into the potential of VR gaming. 
My life is different now.
